card_headline: Egypt heads into the end of its IMF programme with a weak pound, a jailed newsroom and a Rafah crossing open only for small numbers.
card_summary: IMF staff agreed a final review on 19 November that could release about $2.3 billion before the programme expires on 15 December [1]. The government says it will not seek a successor [2]. The pound hit a record 56.39 per dollar in October after the Iran war raised import costs and foreign investors left government debt [1][2]. A court ordered Mada Masr closed on 27 October, and CPJ counts 25 journalists in jail [3][4]. UNHCR counts 1.08 million registered refugees [5].
card_local: Independent local reporting is shrinking: Mada Masr was ordered shut on 27 October, so its own account reached this draft only through other outlets [3]. Al-Manassa reports a $9.7 billion external financing need this fiscal year and privatisation income falling from $3.5 billion to about $400 million [6].
card_international: AP and AFP report Rafah reopening in February and again in March after an Iran-war closure, and Reuters reports mass detentions and deportations of Sudanese refugees [7][8][9]. The National and Al Jazeera cover the IMF deal and the Mada Masr case [1][3].
card_scholar: Carnegie's Yezid Sayigh argues the military's rent-based economy is nearing its limits and leans on foreign borrowing [10]. Chatham House calls Egypt's foreign policy reactive, and the Middle East Institute traces the Iran war's damage to the pound, gas supply and tourism [11][12].
context_md: Egypt has more than 110 million people and takes 55.5 billion cubic metres of Nile water a year, a share Cairo calls existential [13]. Constitutional amendments passed in 2019 allow President Abdel Fattah el-Sisi to stay in office until 2030 [14]. The IMF approved a $3 billion programme in December 2022 and enlarged it to $8 billion in March 2024 [15]. Carnegie's Yezid Sayigh counts about $200 billion in Gulf and international loans, grants and investment from 2013 to 2024, and a further $87 billion in 2024 and 2025 [10]. Suez Canal revenue fell from a record $10.25 billion in 2023 to $3.991 billion in 2024 after Houthi attacks on shipping [16]. A pro-government coalition dominated the parliament elected between November 2025 and January 2026, which had the longest election run in Egypt's modern history [14][17].

sections.title: The IMF programme ends on 15 December and Egypt says it will not ask for another
sections.body_md:
IMF staff reached agreement with Egypt on 19 November on the eighth and final review of its Extended Fund Facility. If the executive board approves, Egypt would receive about $2.3 billion: roughly $1.5 billion from the main facility and up to $800 million from the climate-linked Resilience and Sustainability Facility. Both arrangements expire on 15 December and no board date has been announced [1]. Prime Minister Mostafa Madbouly has said the government does not plan to sign a new IMF agreement [6].

The Fund's tone is cautious. In February it said the sale of state assets was moving slowly and urged faster divestment in non-strategic sectors [18]. Al-Manassa reports that asset sales brought in $3.5 billion in 2025/26 but only about $400 million is expected in 2026/27, against an external financing need of $9.7 billion [6]. Carnegie's Yezid Sayigh projects debt service at 64 percent of proposed 2026/27 state spending [10].

The US-Israeli war on Iran hit Egypt through gas, fuel and capital. Israel shut the Leviathan field on 28 February and resumed deliveries in early April, and fuel prices rose 15 to 22 percent on 10 March, according to the Middle East Institute's Mirette Mabrouk [12]. In October the pound broke 56 per dollar, about $4 billion left government debt between 15 and 26 October, and the central bank raised its rate by 100 basis points to 20 percent [2]. Urban inflation eased to 12.7 percent in October and real growth reached 5.1 percent in 2025/26 [1]. External debt stood at $166.45 billion at end-June, with $60.9 billion due by June 2027 [2].

The Suez Canal is recovering from a low base. August revenue was $567.1 million against $326 million a year earlier, according to Suez Canal Authority chairman Osama Rabie as reported by Egyptian Streets [16]. State-owned Ahram Online reports full-year 2025/26 revenue of $4.6 billion, up 23 percent, while The National puts annual revenue near $4.4 billion, under half the level before the Houthi attacks [19][2].

lenses.local: Al-Manassa reports the financing gap, the privatisation shortfall and parliamentary pushback against a 12 percent electricity price rise [6].
lenses.international: The National reports the IMF agreement and a $1 billion World Bank loan, and says the government absorbed oil at about $110 a barrel rather than pass it on [1][2].
lenses.scholar: Sayigh says the military's rent-extraction model may be saturating, and Mabrouk says Egypt remains exposed to volatile foreign portfolio money [10][12].

sections.title: The crackdown now reaches newsrooms: Mada Masr is closed and a whole fact-checking team is held
sections.body_md:
On 27 October the New Cairo Misdemeanour Court ordered Mada Masr closed and its equipment confiscated, and fined editor-in-chief Lina Attalah 3 million Egyptian pounds for running an unlicensed website under Article 105 of the 2018 media law. Mada Masr says it applied for a licence in 2018 and 2020 without a reply and has had a new application pending since June 2023. Attalah was held for several hours until the fine was paid. There was no immediate official comment [3]. She also faces a retrial on a 2024 in-absentia sentence of one year for false news and unlicensed operation. On 18 November the court suspended that retrial until a request to remove the presiding judge is decided. An appeal hearing on the licensing conviction is set for 25 November and a Court of Appeal panel takes the recusal request on 26 November [20].

Six journalists from the investigative platform Matsadaash were detained on 28 and 29 September [21]. CPJ says they later told prosecutors they were tortured and forced to record false confessions, and that the charges cited include joining and funding terrorism. The Interior Ministry denied the torture claims [4]. CPJ counts 25 journalists in jail, the most since 2021, while the Al-Monitor report on Attalah's interview gives 26 [4][22]. RSF ranks Egypt 169th of 180 countries [23].

The pressure is wider than the press. Human Rights Watch says trials began in May for about 6,000 people referred in terrorism cases, more than half held in pretrial detention for months or years [24]. President Sisi pardoned the activist Alaa Abdel Fattah and five others in September 2025, and Amnesty urged the release of everyone held solely for exercising their rights [25]. No total for political prisoners was found in the sources read here. Official figures put turnout in the House of Representatives election at 32.41 percent, with opposition parties holding 53 of 568 elected seats [17].

lenses.local: Khaled el-Balshy, head of the Journalists' Syndicate, said the union would appeal the closure, and Mada Masr said the court refused to let its lawyers review the case file [3].
lenses.international: CPJ says the arrests form a coordinated campaign and that the United States and European governments have stayed publicly silent [4].
lenses.scholar: TIMEP, a Washington-based policy institute, published a call for the Matsadaash newsroom's release on 30 September and a piece on restrictions on former prisoners on 13 November [26].

sections.title: Rafah reopened in February for small numbers, and Egypt still demands two-way access
sections.body_md:
Israeli troops seized the Palestinian side of the Rafah crossing in May 2024 [7]. In December 2025 Israel said it would open the crossing for exit only, and Egypt rejected that, saying any opening must allow movement in both directions for people and aid [27]. The crossing reopened on 2 February 2026 under EU supervision, with Israel and Egypt vetting travellers, no goods allowed, and caps of about 50 patients leaving and about 50 returnees entering a day, according to AP. Egypt says it fears Israel could use the crossing to push Palestinians out of Gaza [7].

It shut on 28 February when Israel closed all crossings after strikes on Iran, and partly reopened on 19 March, when eight wounded Palestinians and 17 companions crossed into Egypt, according to AFP [8]. For 10 to 16 November, OCHA counts 97 patients, 34 of them children, and 145 companions evacuated through Rafah and Kerem Shalom [28]. In December the UN said at least 16,500 patients needed care abroad, and MSF's Hani Isleem called that a significant underestimate [27].

Aid from Egypt reaches Gaza through Israel's Kerem Shalom crossing. Of 433 UN and partner trucks offloaded there from 9 to 15 November, 127 came from Egypt, after a four-day Israeli suspension of the Egypt route. More than 150,000 tents were waiting outside Gaza as of 13 November, most of them at Al Arish in Egypt [28]. This draft found no AP or Reuters report on Rafah dated after March, so the current daily limits are not confirmed.

lenses.international: AP reports that Egyptian state media confirmed the February reopening and that the Egyptian health ministry prepared hospitals to receive patients [7].
lenses.scholar: Chatham House says Egypt has made itself central to Trump's Gaza plan, works with Qatar and Turkey as mediator, and rejected Israel's exit-only plan [11].

sections.title: Egypt hosts 1.08 million registered refugees and has turned to arrests and deportations of Sudanese
sections.body_md:
UNHCR counted 1,080,336 registered refugees and asylum seekers in Egypt on 31 October 2026. Of these, 843,387 (78.1 percent) are Sudanese and 81,491 are Syrian [5]. Amnesty reported on 16 February that plainclothes police had been arresting refugees since late December 2025, including people holding UNHCR cards, and deporting them without individual risk assessment [29]. The Sudanese ambassador said in January that 207 Sudanese returned in December and 371 in January, and that about 400 were detained, without saying whether the returns were deportations or voluntary [29].

Reuters reported on 24 June that three security officials, speaking anonymously, said more than 5,500 people had been deported since November, against about 100 formal deportations a year in 2023 and 2024. Reuters could not verify the figure. It documented three refugee deaths in custody, and two officials said nine Sudanese had died in custody [9]. UNHCR told Reuters that returns to Sudan should not happen under current conditions. Egypt's State Information Service denied a broad campaign, saying deportations follow legal procedures and apply to people who break the law or pose a security threat, and pointing to its 2024 asylum law [9].

Egypt's position in the Sudan war shapes the politics. Chatham House says Egypt, Turkey and Saudi Arabia back the Sudanese army against the UAE-backed RSF, and that Cairo could intervene if its red lines are crossed [11]. Reuters notes the EU pledged 7.4 billion euros to Egypt in 2024 [9]. Amnesty asks the EU to press Egypt for verifiable protections [29].

lenses.international: Reuters and Amnesty describe overcrowded cells, deaths in custody and families keeping children out of school, and Egypt's State Information Service rejects the picture [9][29].
lenses.scholar: Chatham House frames Egypt's Sudan policy as late and costly, with red lines at the division of Sudan or an RSF advance on the Egyptian border [11].

sections.title: GERD: Egypt blames uncoordinated releases for floods and low flows, and US mediation has produced no talks
sections.body_md:
Egypt's annual Nile share is 55.5 billion cubic metres, and its water per person has fallen from about 2,000 cubic metres a year in the 1960s to under 500, according to figures reported by The New Arab [13]. On 19 July Foreign Minister Badr Abdelatty called water security existential and said Cairo rejects unilateral measures. Egyptian experts said Ethiopia released too little water in July, with daily releases estimated at 150 to 180 million cubic metres. Ethiopia has not confirmed any cut [13].

The 2025 floods are the other half of the dispute. Egypt's Irrigation Ministry accused Ethiopia of reckless dam management and said abrupt discharges worsened flooding in Beheira, Kafr el-Sheikh and Menoufia. Ethiopia says the dam operated under technical protocols and reduced worse flooding in Sudan [30]. The Atlantic Council's Alessia Melcangi describes gaps in data, in operating rules and in trust between the three states, and no binding agreement on filling and operating the dam [30].

Diplomacy has not moved. Trump offered mediation in a January letter to Sisi, and Massad Boulos said in August that Washington would give technical support if talks resume [31][32]. On 9 October Trump said at a rally that Ethiopia had taken the Nile's water, and Ahram Online reported on 13 October that no talks had been confirmed [32]. Egypt criticised remarks by Ethiopia's water minister Habtamu Itefa about building more dams on the Nile [31].

lenses.local: State-owned Ahram Online quotes Salah Halima of the Egyptian Council for African Affairs saying mediation will fail unless Ethiopia shows willingness, and floats a UN referral if all routes fail [32].
lenses.international: Addis Standard reports that Ethiopia rejects limits on its right to develop its water, while Sudan wants regulated flows and cheaper electricity but worries about dam safety [31].
lenses.scholar: Chatham House argues Egypt has lost its historic de facto veto over Nile projects after failing to secure a binding agreement [11].

timeline.text: The IMF approves a $3 billion programme for Egypt.
Suez Canal revenue reaches a record $10.25 billion.
The IMF programme is enlarged to $8 billion.
Israeli troops seize the Palestinian side of the Rafah crossing.
President Sisi pardons Alaa Abdel Fattah and five other prisoners.
Egypt rejects an Israeli plan to open Rafah for exit only and demands two-way movement.
Final results of the House of Representatives election are announced after reruns in annulled constituencies.
Rafah reopens to small numbers of patients and returnees under EU supervision.
Amnesty reports arbitrary arrests and deportations of refugees in Egypt.
Israel closes Gaza crossings and the Leviathan gas field after strikes on Iran, halting gas to Egypt.
Reuters reports surging deportations of Sudanese refugees and deaths in custody.
The IMF completes the seventh review and unlocks about $1.8 billion.
The pound breaks 56 per dollar, a day after a 30-minute halt in trading on the EGX100.
A court orders Mada Masr closed and fines editor Lina Attalah 3 million pounds.
The court suspends Attalah's retrial pending a request to remove the judge.
IMF staff and Egypt agree on the final review of the programme.

scores.coverage_basis: AP, AFP and Reuters copy on Egypt was found for Rafah, refugee deportations and the Mada Masr case, and The National and Al Jazeera follow the IMF talks and the press cases [7][9][3][1]. Coverage spikes when Gaza, the IMF or a court ruling makes news, and independent local reporting is shrinking as Mada Masr is closed [4].

severity.basis: This draft did not examine ACLED or UCDP data on Egypt. The violence found is spillover and custodial: Reuters documented three refugee deaths in custody, and Gaza's humanitarian crisis sits on the border [9][28].
Egypt hosts 1.08 million registered refugees, and subsidies cost about 840 billion pounds this fiscal year while food prices rise [5][2].
CPJ counts 25 journalists jailed, the highest since 2021, a newsroom was detained and Mada Masr was ordered closed, and RSF ranks Egypt 169th of 180 [4][3][23].
External debt is $166.45 billion, debt service takes 64 percent of the proposed budget, and the pound hit a record low in October, though inflation is falling and growth is 5.1 percent [2][10][1].
The press crackdown escalated in September and October and the pound hit a record in October, while inflation fell from 13.9 to 12.7 percent and growth reached 5.1 percent [4][2][1].

parts.basis: The US has offered to mediate on the Nile, the UAE and Qatar have committed $35 billion and $29.7 billion to coastal developments, and the EU pledged 7.4 billion euros in 2024 [31][10][9].

Suez Canal revenue fell from $10.25 billion in 2023 to about $4.4 billion a year, and Israel supplies 15 to 20 percent of Egypt's gas, so a Red Sea or Leviathan stoppage is felt in shipping and energy markets [16][2][12].
Egypt borders Gaza and takes Sudanese refugees, and the Nile dispute remains without an agreement [7][5][31].
Egypt has more than 110 million people, hosts 1.08 million registered refugees and received record remittances of $33.9 billion in the first eight months of the year [13][5][2].

Amnesty says deportations breach non-refoulement and Egypt's own asylum law, and no binding agreement governs the GERD, while Chatham House lists the Israel peace treaty among Cairo's priorities [29][30][11].

summary: Egypt matters beyond its borders through the Rafah crossing, the Suez Canal and the Nile. Gaza aid and medical evacuations pass through Egyptian territory, and Suez Canal revenue ran at $10.25 billion in 2023 before the Red Sea attacks [28][16].

The score stays below the top tier because Egypt's own conflict risk is low in the sources read and its great-power ties are mostly financial and diplomatic. Chatham House calls Egypt's foreign policy reactive and sidelined as Washington prioritises Israel and the Gulf [11].
gi.up: A collapse of the Gaza ceasefire or renewed Houthi attacks on Red Sea shipping would raise it.
gi.down: A signed Nile agreement and a durable return of container lines to Suez would lower it.

gaps: Local sourcing is thin: Mada Masr's own pages were not opened and its account is read through Al Jazeera, The National and CPJ; Al-Manassa's August piece was read once and its search listing carried a generic title.

Ahram Online pages on the Suez FY2025/26 figure, the GERD data blackout and Gaza aid convoys failed to open. The $4.6 billion Suez figure rests on a headline seen in search results, and Ahram is state-owned.
The 5.1 percent growth headline from Egypt Independent was seen in search results only; the figure is confirmed by The National.
The two Suez revenue figures ($4.6 billion for the fiscal year and about $4.4 billion a year) were not reconciled.
No Crisis Group page on Egypt was opened. TIMEP's site was read as a listing only, so its November pieces on former political prisoners and the IMF were not read.
No total count of political prisoners was found; HRW gives none. The Presidential Pardon Committee and the status of Alaa Abdel Fattah after September 2025 were not researched.
Violence data (ACLED, UCDP) and Sinai security were not examined, so the violence score is low-confidence.
Rafah: no AP or Reuters story after March 2026 was found; the November picture rests on one OCHA report and current daily caps are unconfirmed.

The 5,500 deportation figure rests on three anonymous officials via Reuters. UNHCR's registered total fell from 1,099,024 in January (per Amnesty) to 1,080,336 in October; the reason was not established.
The Matsadaash funding fact-check rests on CPJ alone; CPJ's earlier alert reported no formal charges and its later report lists terrorism charges, so the exact charge sheet is unconfirmed.
No outcome is available for the Mada Masr hearings of 25 and 26 November as of 25 November.
No podcast episode or documentary was verified for this draft, and the GERD flow estimates for July come from Egyptian experts without Ethiopian confirmation.
